Zafar Khan was an Afghan adventurer who rose to prominence during a massive rebellion of the Amiran-i-Sada (centurion nobles) against the oppressive policies of the Delhi Sultan, Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Upon successfully establishing the independent empire, Zafar Khan ascended the throne under the regal title Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah.

He is widely remembered in historical folklore by his earlier name, Hasan Gangu. According to the 16th-century chronicler Firishta, “Gangu” was the name of a Brahmin astrologer in Delhi who had originally employed Hasan and prophesied his future kingship, though modern historians often debate the literal accuracy of this legend.

Ismail Mukh (an elderly and respected Afghan noble) was actually the first leader chosen by the rebel amirs in the Deccan, briefly taking the title Nasir-udDin Ismail Shah. However, realising he lacked the military vigour to fend off the Delhi imperial army, he voluntarily abdicated the throne in favour of the much more capable Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu).

Mahmud Gawan: While he is arguably the most famous figure of the Bahmani era, he was not the founder. He was a brilliant Persian merchant who later served as the Prime Minister (Vakil-usSultanat) under Muhammad Shah III, taking the empire to its absolute territorial and cultural zenith in the late 15th century.

20

Quli Qutb Shah: He was a later provincial governor of the Bahmani Empire who declared independence after the empire’s fragmentation in the 16th century, founding the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda.

Additional facts:

3 First capital: Upon founding the empire, Hasan Gangu established his capital at Gulbarga (which he renamed Ahsanabad). The capital was later shifted to Bidar by Ahmad Shah Wali in the 1420s.

3 To consolidate his vast new territory, Hasan Gangu divided his empire into four primary provinces called Tarafs (Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar, and Bidar), placing each under the strict military and administrative control of a loyal governor (Tarafdar).

questions.q: In the seventeenth century, Bihar was globally important for exporting which key ingredient used in gunpowder?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Saltpetre was the critical oxidative ingredient for manufacturing gunpowder. During the 17th century, the heavily nitrated soils of Bihar (centred strategically around Patna and Chapra) yielded the highest quality and volume of saltpetre globally, prompting intense commercial rivalry between European joint-stock companies seeking to secure the supply chain for their domestic militaries.

Additional facts:

3 The physical extraction, lixiviation (washing), and preliminary refining of saltpetre from the nitrate-rich topsoil of Bihar were exclusively performed by a specialised, marginalised indigenous peasant caste historically known as the Nunias.

3 To consolidate their lucrative supply chain, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) established a massive, highly efficient saltpetre refinery at Chapra, while the English East India Company (EIC officially appointed Job Charnock as the chief of their Patna factory in 1658 to secure direct procurement.

3 The astronomical surge in European demand for Bihar’s saltpetre during this specific period was directly fueled by the intense, continentwide military conflicts transforming European statecraft, most notably the Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648) and the English Civil War.

3 Due to the vast quantities required, refined saltpetre was transported in bulk via flatbottomed heavy river barges (patellas) down the Ganges River to the deep-water port of Hugli in Bengal, where it was loaded onto heavily armed European East Indiamen.

3 Recognising the extreme strategic military value of the chemical, the Mughal state, particularly under Emperor Aurangzeb, periodically imposed strict export embargoes on saltpetre to prevent European entities from stockpiling munitions during regional hostilities, such as the Anglo-Mughal War (Child’s War) in 1689.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Shivaji’s coronation: 1. Gangabhatt of Varanasi officiated the coronation ceremony. 2. Shivaji adopted the title Haindava Dharmoddharak. 3. Instead of ending Chauth, acquiring independent sovereign status gave Shivaji the legal authority to formally demand this 25 percent territorial tax, alongside Sardeshmukhi, from rival domains without being labelled a subordinate rebel.

Additional facts:

3 Shivaji held a supplementary coronation on September 24, 1674, overseen by Nischal Puri Goswami using Tantric rituals to ward off perceived bad omens following his mother Jijabai’s death.

3 To mark the beginning of his independent royal administration, Shivaji introduced a new calendar era known as the Rajyabhisheka Shaka.

questions.q: Under which ruler did Jaunpur become known as the “Shiraz of the East”?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Jaunpur reached its highest peak of cultural, literary, and architectural brilliance under Sultan Ibrahim Shah Sharqi. His extensive royal patronage attracted thousands of Islamic scholars, Sufis, poets, and artists who had fled the devastation of Delhi during Timur’s invasion. This massive influx of intellect transformed the provincial capital into the premier centre of Islamic learning in northern India, earning it the celebrated title “Shiraz of the East.”

Additional facts:

3 The Sharqi (Eastern) dynasty was originally founded by Malik Sarwar, a powerful noble and eunuch who served as the Wazir under the later Tughlaqs before exploiting the political vacuum to declare independence.

3 Ibrahim Shah Sharqi was responsible for the completion of the Atala Masjid in 1408. This monument defined the distinct “Jaunpur style” of architecture, which is heavily characterised by massive sloping walls, square pillars, intricate stone screens, and a prominent absence of minarets.

3 The independent Sharqi kingdom was eventually extinguished and permanently reannexed into the Delhi Sultanate after Bahlul Lodi decisively defeated its final ruler, Husain Shah Sharqi (who was himself a renowned patron of classical music and credited with developing/popularising the Khayal style).

questions.q: Which Chola temple is popularly known as “Dakshina Meru”?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Brihadeshwara Temple, built by the Chola ruler Rajaraja I at Thanjavur around 1010 CE, is popularly known as “Dakshina Meru” (Southern Meru). The name reflects its massive pyramidal vimana (tower), symbolically compared to Mount Meru, the sacred cosmic mountain in Indian tradition. Its 13-storeyed vimana rises to about 60 metres and is one of the tallest temple towers of medieval India.

The temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is also called Rajarajesvaram.

It is the finest example of mature Chola architecture and is now part of the UNESCO-listed Great Living Chola Temples.

Gangaikonda Cholapuram Temple was built by Rajendra I and is another major Chola temple’

Airavatesvara Temple was built by Rajaraja II and is known for its exquisite stone carvings.

Nageswaraswamy Temple is located at Kumbakonam and represents the Early Chola architectural phase (attributed to Aditya I), famous for its life-size, hyper-realistic external portrait sculptures.

questions.q: In Shivaji’s Ashtapradhan Mandal, which official handled finance and audited accounts?

Option A is incorrect: Sumant, previously known by the Persian title Dabir, functioned as the foreign minister of the Maratha state. This official was strictly responsible for managing diplomatic relations, receiving foreign envoys, and advising Chhatrapati Shivaji on strategic alliances and conflicts with neighbouring powers like the Mughal Empire and Bijapur.

Option B is incorrect: Sachiv, formerly known as the Shurnis, was the superintendent of royal correspondence. This minister’s primary role was to draft and dispatch royal edicts (farmans), affix the official seal to documents, and maintain the textual accuracy of state letters. They reviewed the registers of specific administrative districts (parganas).

Option C is correct: Amatya, previously titled Majumdar, served directly as the finance minister of the Maratha administration. This official was responsible for auditing all public accounts of the kingdom, monitoring imperial income and expenditure, and specifically counter-signing all state financial documents to maintain economic stability and prevent administrative fraud.

Option D is incorrect: Peshwa, or Mukhya Pradhan, acted as the Prime Minister and the highest-ranking official in the Ashtapradhan Mandal. Peshwa oversaw the general administration of the empire and could deputise for the Chhatrapati during his absence or in military campaigns.

22

Additional facts:

3 All ministers within the council, with the strict exception of the Panditrao (head of religious affairs) and the Nyayadhish (chief justice), were militarily obligated to command armies and lead expeditions during wartime.

3 To prevent the rise of a rebellious feudal aristocracy, Shivaji strictly paid these eight ministers through direct cash salaries (nagad) from the state treasury rather than granting them autonomous land assignments (jagirs or saranjams).

3 Ramchandra Pant Amatya, who served as the Amatya and later the Hukumatpanah, authored the Adnyapatra, a highly influential Marathi treatise detailing Maratha statecraft, naval policy, and fort architecture.

3 Each primary minister was administratively supported by a standardised departmental staff of eight clerks, which included specific roles like the Diwan (chief secretary) and Phadnis (deputy auditor).

3 The transition from Persian administrative titles (such as Majumdar and Dabir) to their Sanskrit equivalents (Amatya and Sumant) was officially executed during Shivaji’s 1674 coronation to align with his Haindava Dharmoddharak ideology.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Mahmud Gawan: 1. He increased the number of provinces from four to eight to limit the power of governors. 2. He abolished khalisa lands and gave all revenue to military commanders. 3. He kept at least one major fort in each province under central control. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 2 is incorrect: Mahmud Gawan did not abolish the Khalisa lands. To curb the financial independence of the powerful nobles, he significantly expanded the Khalisa (tracts of land whose revenue went directly to the Sultan’s central treasury) by carving them out of the provincial territories.

Statements 1 and 3 are correct: Gawan recognised that the vast original four provinces (established by Hasan Gangu) made the governors (tarafdars) dangerously powerful. He divided them into eight smaller provinces. Furthermore, he systematically stripped the governors of their absolute military monopoly by placing at least one major fort in each province under the direct control of an officer appointed by the Sultan (Qiladar).

Additional facts:

3 Gawan was not a native noble. He was a Persian merchant (an Afaqi or Gharib) who rose to become the Vakil-us-Sultanat (Prime Minister) under Muhammad Shah III.

3 He heavily modernised the Bahmani military, employing Persian and Turkish chemists to introduce the organised use of gunpowder and artillery in the Deccan.

3 He built a magnificent, Persian-style Madrasa at Bidar, which became a premier Islamic university equipped with a massive library of 3,000 manuscripts.

3 His centralising reforms deeply angered the older, native nobility (the Deccanis). They forged a treasonous letter implicating Gawan in a conspiracy, leading the intoxicated Sultan to order his execution in 1481, an event that triggered the rapid fragmentation of the Bahmani Empire.

questions.q: In the Mughal Jagirdari system, what were Watan Jagirs?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Transferable revenue assignments to Turani nobles changed every three years
options.B: Non-transferable hereditary lands given to Rajput rulers in their own territories
options.C: Lands directly managed by the imperial treasury for the Emperor
options.D: Charitable land grants to religious scholars and Sufis

questions.explanation:
Option B is the correct: Watan Jagirs were a highly specialised category of non-transferable, hereditary land grants specifically designed to pragmatically accommodate subjugated Rajput chieftains (and later other prominent local Zamindars), allowing them to retain autonomous administrative control over their ancestral territories in exchange for formally acknowledging Mughal suzerainty and providing military service.

Option A is incorrect: Standard revenue assignments granted to regular Mughal nobles (such as the Turanis, Iranis, or Indian Muslims) in lieu of cash salaries were simply known as standard Jagirs, and these were deliberately made transferable every three to four years by the imperial centre to strictly prevent the nobility from establishing entrenched, autonomous power bases in any single province.

Option C is incorrect: Lands whose revenue was reserved directly for the imperial treasury rather than being assigned to nobles were classified as Khalisa, and the massive income generated from these highly productive territories was utilised specifically to maintain the emperor’s personal household, the royal court, and his direct standing army (such as the Ahadis).

Option D is incorrect: Tax-free, charitable land grants bestowed upon religious scholars, destitute widows, and Sufi mystics for their daily sustenance were legally classified as Madad-iMa’ash or Suyurghal, and unlike standard jagirs, these grants were typically held for life and were fundamentally divorced from any required military or administrative obligations to the state.

23

Additional facts:

3 A Jagirdar was never granted actual proprietary ownership of the land itself; the imperial assignment solely conferred the right to collect the state’s share of the land revenue and associated local taxes from the peasantry within that specific jurisdiction.

3 The imperial revenue administration strictly maintained two separate financial metrics for these assignments: the Jama (the officially estimated revenue calculated by the state on paper) and the Hasil (the actual revenue practically collected by the noble on the ground).

3 During the later decades of Aurangzeb’s reign, the massive expansion of the nobility following the Deccan campaigns, combined with a severe shortage of productive unassigned land (Pai-baqi), directly triggered the famous “Jagirdari crisis,” where the Hasil fell drastically below the Jama, effectively crippling the nobles’ financial ability to maintain their required cavalry contingents.

3 To ensure the Jagirdars did not illegally extort or oppress the peasantry while collecting their assigned revenue, the Mughal state appointed independent imperial officers directly accountable to the centre, such as the Faujdar (military commander) and the Amal-guzar (revenue collector), to heavily monitor local administrative practices within the jagirs.

questions.q: Consider the following pairs regarding the ministers of the Ashtapradhan Mandal: 1. Sumant Managed foreign affairs 2. Senapati Commanded the imperial military forces 3. Nyayadhish Supervised the drafting of the royal correspondence. 4. Panditrao Granted state charities to religious scholars and temples. How many pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correct: The Sumant (Persian title: Dabir) functioned as the foreign minister, responsible for receiving envoys and managing external diplomacy.

Pair 2 is correct: The Senapati (Persian title: Sar-iNaubat) served directly as the commander-in-chief of the Maratha military. This official organised troop recruitment, maintained army discipline, and held the primary responsibility of leading major expeditionary campaigns against the Mughal Empire and the Adil Shahi Sultanate.

Pair 3 is incorrect: Nyayadhish acted as the chief justice, resolving civil and criminal disputes based on Hindu legal texts (Smritis). The actual supervision of royal correspondence, drafting state letters, and affixing the official seal (muhur) was the specific duty of the Sachiv (Persian title: Shurnis).

Pair 4 is correct: The Panditrao (Persian equivalent: Sadar) headed the religious administration of the state. This minister was specifically tasked with overseeing theological disputes, honouring religious scholars, and distributing state-funded charities and land grants (inams) to temples and Brahmins.

Additional facts:

3 The council did not function as an independent, modern cabinet; all eight ministers acted strictly as advisory secretaries who executed Chhatrapati Shivaji’s direct royal orders.

3 Except for the Nyayadhish and Panditrao, the remaining six state ministers were legally obligated to command military contingents and lead wartime expeditions.

3 To prevent regional rebellions, the Maratha state paid these ministers direct cash salaries (nagad) from the central treasury, strictly prohibiting the assignment of hereditary land grants (jagirs).

3 The Peshwa (Mukhya Pradhan) acted as the prime minister, coordinating all state departments, and was the sole minister authorised to deputise for the king during his physical absence.

3 During the 1674 coronation, Shivaji systematically replaced the Persian administrative titles of these ministers (such as Majumdar and Dabir) with Sanskrit equivalents (like Amatya and Sumant).

questions.q: The hill-top Vikramshila University, founded by Dharmapala, was located in which region?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Dharmapala founded the Vikramasila University to expand Buddhist learning in eastern India. The institution was strategically located at the top of a hill on the banks of the Ganga River in the Magadha region.

Additional Facts:

3 While it was a premier centre of learning, historical and textual records indicate it became second only to Nalanda in international fame.

3 The foundation of the university was accompanied by extensive construction; the Palas built many viharas (monasteries) in which a large number of Buddhist monks lived.

3 Kamrup (Assam) was a region Devapala expanded into, Malwa was contested by the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, and Tirhut (north Bengal) was a distinct territory mentioned later in the Sultanate period.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Balban: 1. Ziauddin Barani’s works describe the destruction of the Chahalgani by Balban. 2. Balban used strong military action to suppress the Mewatis. 3. He promoted non-Turkish nobles to replace the old Turkish nobles. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: According to Barani, Balban, who was himself a former member of this

24

elite Turkish slave nobility established by Iltutmish, understood that the Sultan’s absolute authority could never be secure as long as these powerful nobles existed. Balban used a mix of espionage, harsh punishments for minor transgressions (as seen in the brutal public floggings of Malik Baqbaq and Haibat Khan), and covert assassinations (such as the suspected poisoning of his cousin, Sher Khan) to entirely annihilate the political influence of his former peers.

Statement 2 is correct: Balban’s “Blood and Iron” policy was the operationalisation of extreme state violence to restore the prestige and writ of the Crown. As recorded in the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi, the Doab region and the immediate outskirts of Delhi were plagued by highway robbers and rebellious Rajput groups, particularly the Mewatis, who routinely plundered the capital. Balban responded with ruthless military suppression: he ordered the clearing of dense forests that served as rebel hideouts, established military outposts (thanas) manned by Afghan soldiers, and slaughtered thousands of rebels, effectively securing the capital and reopening trade routes.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Balban did not elevate indigenous non-Turkish nobles; in fact, he was a staunch elitist who aggressively championed the racial supremacy of pure-blooded Turks. Barani mentions Balban’s intense disdain for low-born individuals, famously recording the Sultan’s declaration that seeing a man of base origin caused his hand to instinctively reach for his sword. Instead of replacing the Chahalgani with Indian Muslims or commoners (a policy later adopted by the Khaljis), Balban relied strictly on elevating his own dynastic prestige and centralising military power to fill the vacuum left by the destroyed aristocracy. He summarily dismissed officials like Kamal Mahiyar simply because of their indigenous, non-aristocratic lineages. Additional facts:

To philosophically justify his despotic rule and elevate himself above the remaining nobility, Balban adopted ancient Persian concepts of monarchy. He declared the Sultan to be the Zilli-Ilahi (the Shadow of God on Earth) and the Niyabat-i-Khudai (the Deputy of God), asserting that his power was derived directly from the divine, not from the consensus of the nobles.

He introduced rigid, highly formal Persian court protocols, most notably Sijda (prostration before the monarch) and Paibos (kissing the Sultan’s feet). These rituals were specifically designed to break the pride of the Turkish nobles and enforce total physical submission to the Crown. He also introduced the celebration of the Persian New Year festival, Nauroz, to project imperial splendour.

Recognising that his “Blood and Iron” policy required a highly efficient standing army independent of the nobles’ feudal levies, Balban separated the military department from the financial department (Diwani-Wazarat). He established the Diwan-i-Arz and placed it under the command of a highly competent and trusted officer, Imad-ul-Mulk, who served as the Ariz-i-Mumalik.

To preempt rebellions and monitor the activities of ambitious nobles and local administrators, Balban instituted a pervasive and highly organised espionage system. Spies (Barids) were placed in every province and department. They functioned independently of provincial governors and reported directly to the Sultan; failure to report a nobleman’s transgression resulted in the spy’s own execution.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Mughal defeat at the Battle of Kannauj in 1540 resulted in the collapse of the newly established Mughal Empire in India. Reason (R): Humayun’s brothers Kamran and Hindal betrayed him during the battle by actively fighting on the side of Sher Shah’s Afghan forces. Select the correct answer:
questions.question_type: Assertion and Reason — Standard Relationship Evaluation

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation:
Assertion (A) is true: The Battle of Kannauj was a decisive encounter. Humayun lost his entire army in this battle. He was forced to flee from Agra and Delhi. This event marked the temporary end of Mughal rule in India. It initiated the fifteen-year Sur Interregnum.

Reason (R) is false: Kamran and Hindal did not fight for Sher Shah. They simply refused to cooperate with Humayun. Kamran withdrew his battlehardened troops to Lahore before the clash. This lack of unity crippled Mughal military strength. The brothers did not commit direct battlefield treason at Kannauj.

Additional facts:

3 The Battle of Kannauj is also known as the Battle of Bilgram.

3 Humayun’s army suffered from severe demoralisation and poor organisation.

3 Heavy rains disrupted the Mughal camp setup.

3 Sher Shah pursued Humayun relentlessly into the Punjab.

3 Humayun eventually sought refuge in Safavid Persia.

3 Shah Tahmasp I eventually provided Humayun with military support.

25

questions.q: Consider the following pairs of Bahmani successor dynasties and their capital Sultanates: 1. Adil Shahi Bijapur 2. Nizam Shahi Bidar 3. Qutb Shahi Golconda 4. Imad Shahi Ahmadnagar How many pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.question_type: Numerical/Calculation — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Pair 1 is correctly matched: The Adil Shahi dynasty was founded by Yusuf Adil Shah and ruled the Sultanate of Bijapur.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched: The Nizam Shahi dynasty, founded by Malik Ahmad, ruled the Sultanate of Ahmadnagar. Bidar was ruled by the Barid Shahi dynasty.

Pair 3 is correctly matched: The Qutb Shahi dynasty, founded by Quli Qutb Shah, ruled the wealthy Sultanate of Golconda.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched: The Imad Shahi dynasty, founded by Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, ruled the Sultanate of Berar.

Additional facts:

3 The fragmentation of the Bahmani Empire began shortly after the unjust execution of its brilliant Prime Minister, Mahmud Gawan, in 1481, which sparked intense infighting between the Deccani (native) and Afaqi (foreign) nobles.

3 Berar (Imad Shahi) was the first to declare independence (1490), but it was also the first to be extinguished when it was annexed by its neighbour, Ahmadnagar, in 1574.

3 Bijapur and Golconda were the most powerful and the longest-lasting of the five sultanates. They survived for nearly two centuries until they were finally conquered and annexed into the Mughal Empire by Aurangzeb in 1686 and 1687, respectively.

3 These sultanates became distinct, magnificent centres of Dakhni culture. The Qutb Shahis built the Charminar in Hyderabad, and the Adil Shahis constructed the Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur (which possesses one of the largest domes in the world).

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Mansabdari system during the reign of Akbar: 1. The Zat rank established the personal status of the official and determined his individual cash salary. 2. A mansabdar was categorised as a first-class noble if his Sawar rank was exactly equal to his Zat rank. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Zat rank functioned as the primary indicator of a noble’s personal position and hierarchical status within the vast imperial Mughal administration, directly dictating his personal cash remuneration and standing at the imperial court.

Statement 2 is correct: Akbar structurally categorised his mansabdars into three distinct tiers within each numerical grade, classifying a noble as first-class if his Sawar rank was exactly equal to his Zat rank, second-class if it was half or more, and third-class if the Sawar rank fell strictly below half of his Zat rank.

Additional facts:

3 The Mansabdari framework was formally institutionalised into a dual-rank system (Zat and Sawar) during the 40th regnal year of Akbar (1595–1596), replacing the tribal and hereditary structures of the earlier nobility with a purely merit-based bureaucracy.

3 To prevent military fraud and ensure the accurate maintenance of the Sawar rank (which dictated the exact number of cavalrymen a noble had to maintain), Akbar heavily enforced the Dagh (branding of horses) and Chehra (descriptive rolls of soldiers) systems, a practice originally pioneered by Alauddin Khalji and Sher Shah Suri.

3 Salaries were disbursed either in direct cash (Naqdi) from the imperial treasury or, more commonly, through non-hereditary territorial revenue assignments known as Jagirs, which were subject to frequent administrative transfers to prevent the nobles from establishing entrenched local power bases.

3 Unlike European feudalism, the system was strictly non-hereditary due to the rigorous application of the law of escheat, which mandated that upon the death of a mansabdar, all his personal wealth and assigned jagirs automatically reverted to the imperial state.

questions.q: What concession did Balaji Vishwanath obtain in Delhi in 1719?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Grant of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi over six Deccan provinces
options.B: Recognition of Maratha sovereignty over Malwa
options.C: Right to mint imperial silver in Shahu’s name
options.D: Transfer of Gujarat ports to Marathas

questions.explanation:
Option A is correct: In 1719, Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath secured three historic imperial edicts (farmans) brokered by the powerful Sayyid brothers. This officially granted Chhatrapati Shahu the legal right to extract Chauth (25% of revenue) and Sardeshmukhi (an additional 10%) from the six Mughal provinces (subahs) of the Deccan. This monumental agreement formally transitioned the Maratha state from a rebel faction into a legally recognised tributary power within the Mughal system.

Option B is incorrect: The recognition of Maratha dominance over the Malwa province was not achieved in 1719. The formal imperial cession of Malwa occurred much later in 1741 under Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao, following the aggressive military campaigns previously launched by Baji Rao I across the Narmada River.

26

Option C is incorrect: The 1719 agreement strictly recognised Shahu as a high-ranking vassal, not an independent emperor. It did not grant the Marathas the sovereign right to mint imperial Mughal silver (rupiya) in Shahu’s name, as such an act would directly challenge the core sovereignty of the Mughal throne.

Option D is incorrect: The treaty strictly covered the internal Deccan provinces and explicitly excluded Gujarat. Maratha control over Gujarat and its lucrative coastal ports was systematically established in the subsequent decades by independent military commanders like Khanderao Dabhade and the Gaikwad clan.

Additional facts:

3 As a primary condition for collecting these revenues, Shahu was legally obligated to maintain a permanent contingent of 15,000 Maratha cavalry for imperial Mughal service in the Deccan.

3 In exchange for the Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rights, the Maratha administration agreed to pay a fixed annual tribute of ten lakh rupees to the central Mughal treasury.

3 A crucial diplomatic victory of this treaty was the secure release of Shahu’s mother, Yesubai, who had remained a Mughal political hostage since the capture of Raigad fort in 1689.

3 Balaji Vishwanath marched with a force of 15,000 Maratha soldiers to Delhi alongside Sayyid Husain Ali Khan, playing a direct military role in the deposition of Emperor Farrukhsiyar.

3 The British historian Richard Temple famously termed these 1719 imperial edicts the “Magna Carta of the Maratha Dominion” because they provided the ultimate legal foundation for the Maratha Confederacy.

questions.q: Which large mosque built at Pandua by Sikandar Shah of the Ilyas Shahi dynasty is considered the biggest in medieval India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
The Adina Mosque was built in 1374 by Sikandar Shah to project the imperial majesty of the newly independent Bengal Sultanate after successfully defending his territory against the invasions of the Delhi Sultanate (under Firoz Shah Tughlaq).

Additional facts:

3 The dynasty was founded by Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah in 1342. He achieved the historic milestone of uniting the three warring principalities of Lakhnauti, Sonargaon, and Satgaon into a singular geopolitical and cultural entity known as Bangalah.

3 The Ilyas Shahi rulers fiercely maintained political independence from Delhi and actively fostered a distinct Bengali cultural identity by extending royal patronage to both Persian scholars and indigenous Bengali literature.

3 The Bengal architectural style heavily utilised local brick and intricate terracotta ornamentation due to the lack of stone. Its most defining feature is the “curved cornice” (a drooping roofline), directly adapted from traditional Bengali bamboo huts to quickly drain heavy monsoon rain.

3 Alongside the Adina Mosque, the other defining structure of this era is the Eklakhi Mausoleum at Pandua, built by the Sultan Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah. It serves as the earliest surviving prototype of the square, single-domed brick tomb in Bengal.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Maratha taxation system: 1. Chauth was one-fourth of the assessed land revenue. 2. Sardeshmukhi was an additional ten percent claimed as hereditary right. 3. Payment of Chauth brought the territory under Maratha administration. Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Chauth was a mandatory military tribute exacted by the Maratha state, representing exactly one-fourth (25 percent) of the standard land revenue assessment of a targeted region. Shivaji legally justified this collection from neighbouring Mughal and Adil Shahi provinces as a necessary protection fee to guarantee those territories’ absolute immunity from Maratha cavalry raids.

Statement 2 is correct: Sardeshmukhi was an extra 10 percent revenue surcharge levied strictly in addition to the Chauth. Shivaji claimed this specific exaction based on his legal assertion of being the premier, hereditary Sardeshmukh (chief revenue collector) of Maharashtra, utilising the tax to assert his supreme sovereign authority over all other regional landlords (zamindars and deshmukhs).

Statement 3 is incorrect: Paying Chauth functioned strictly as a military protection treaty, essentially a ransom to prevent Maratha invasions. It did not result in political annexation, nor did it transfer the internal civil administration, local law enforcement, or regional judicial authority of the paying territory into the Maratha imperial state apparatus.

Additional facts:

3 The earliest documented instance of Shivaji successfully demanding Chauth occurred in 1665 from the rural districts of the Mughal province of Khandesh.

27

3 During the later Peshwa era, the Chauth was systematically divided into four shares: Babti (25% for the Chhatrapati), Sahotra (6% for the Sachiv), Nadgaunda (3% for royal grants), and Mokasa (66% assigned to military commanders to maintain troops).

3 Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar formally legitimised the Maratha right to exact both Chauth and Sardeshmukhi across the six Mughal provinces of the Deccan in 1719, following a treaty brokered by the Sayyid brothers.

3 The Maratha administration appointed specific regional revenue agents known as Gumashtas to formally audit and collect the Sardeshmukhi dues from subdued foreign territories.

3 The financial calculation for these external tributes was heavily reliant on the existing Mughal standard revenue assessments originally formalised by Todar Mal, rather than requiring fresh Maratha land surveys.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the Ayagar system in the Vijayanagara Empire?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: A centralised system with officials transferred and paid cash salaries by the state
options.B: A village system with twelve hereditary functionaries paid through tax-free land
options.C: A system where village heads maintained cavalry for the ruler
options.D: An urban guild system for trade and price control

questions.explanation:
Statement B is correct: The Ayagar system was the fundamental bedrock of local village administration in the Vijayanagara Empire. It consisted of a body of twelve village functionaries (Ayagars), including the headman (Gouda), accountant (Karnam), watchman (Talari), and various artisans.

In exchange for their services to the village community, they were granted tax-free lands (often termed Manya or Umbali) and a fixed share of the agricultural harvest.

questions.q: Which term referred to state-run urban workshops producing luxury goods for the Mughal court?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
In the Mughal administrative system, Karkhanas functioned as highly specialised imperial manufacturing centres where skilled artisans operated directly under state supervision to produce high-quality luxury items such as silk textiles, fine jewellery, and ornate weaponry exclusively for the royal court.

Additional facts:

3 The prominent 17th-century French physician and traveller François Bernier provided extensive contemporary documentation regarding the internal organisation and scale of these imperial workshops.

3 To ensure absolute quality control and mitigate independent commercial risk, the central administration supplied raw materials directly to the state-employed artisans.

3 Unlike independent village craftsmen, the specialised artisans operating within the imperial Karkhanas received regular, guaranteed cash wages from the state treasury.

3 These institutional workshops also functioned as vital centres for generational skill transmission, where master craftsmen rigorously trained young apprentices in highly specialised trades.

3 The Karkhanas were specifically responsible for manufacturing the magnificent imperial robes of honour (khilat) routinely bestowed by the emperor upon prominent nobles and foreign dignitaries.

3 Crucially, these state-sponsored workshops operated entirely outside the traditional economy and strictly did not produce goods for sale on the open commercial market.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Varkari saints: 1. Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita. 2. Eknath composed the Dasbodh, a sociopolitical text unifying Marathas. 3. Tukaram’s abhangas promoted equality and challenged caste hierarchy. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Dnyaneshwar (also spelled Jnaneshwar) was a thirteenth-century poet-saint. He authored the Dnyaneshwari around 1290 CE. It is a Marathi-language philosophical commentary on the Bhagavad Gita. It is considered the foundational text of the Varkari literary tradition.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Dasbodh was not composed by Eknath. It was authored by Swami Ramdas. Swami Ramdas belonged to the entirely distinct Samarth sect, not the Varkari tradition. Eknath was a sixteenth-century Varkari saint. Eknath is celebrated for his social reform work, particularly his outreach to lower castes and untouchables. He also produced the Eknathi Bhagavata, a Marathi commentary on the eleventh canto of the Bhagavata Purana.

Statement 3 is correct: Tukaram was a seventeenthcentury Varkari saint. He composed abhangas (short devotional verses) in Marathi. His compositions carried a consistently egalitarian social message. He openly criticised Brahminical ritual exclusivity. His teachings helped unify diverse social groups under a common devotional identity. This directly contributed to the broader social cohesion that enabled Shivaji’s Swarajya.

Additional facts:

3 The Varkari (Pilgrim) socio-religious movement geographically and spiritually centered entirely on the biannual vari pilgrimage

28

to the Vithoba (Vitthal) temple complex at Pandharpur, situated on the banks of the Bhima (Chandrabhaga) river in Maharashtra.

3 Namdev, a prominent 14th-century Shudra tailor and early Varkari saint-poet, traveled extensively into the Punjab; acknowledging his profound spiritual impact, 61 of his devotional hymns were later officially canonized within the Sikh holy scripture, the Adi Granth (Guru Granth Sahib).

3 To systematically dismantle the elitist, Sanskrit-dominated orthodox religious monopoly, Varkari saints exclusively utilized the vernacular Marathi language, specifically popularizing the Ovi and Abhanga poetic meters to democratise spiritual access for the marginalized agrarian and artisanal classes.

3 Saint Eknath aggressively challenged deeply entrenched caste orthodoxy by publicly dining with untouchables (Mahars) and utilizing the indigenous Bharud (folk drama-poem) format to effectively disseminate socio-spiritual reforms among the illiterate rural masses.

3 The prolonged period of Varkari-driven cultural, spiritual, and linguistic unification across severe caste divides directly established the foundational socio-political cohesion that Chhatrapati Shivaji later harnessed to mobilize the Maratha Swarajya.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur is incorrect?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct

options.A: It has a Whispering Gallery where faint sounds echo clearly.
options.B: The central dome is supported by internal load-bearing pillars
options.C: It is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah.
options.D: It uses eight intersecting arches to support the dome.

questions.explanation:
Statement B is incorrect: The most remarkable engineering achievement of the Gol Gumbaz is that it does not use any internal pillars to support the dome. Instead, it utilises a brilliant system of eight intersecting arches (known as pendentives) created by the overlapping of two rotated squares. This specific design supports the massive dome while leaving the interior as one giant, uninterrupted open space.

The structure was built to be a grand tomb for Muhammad Adil Shah and is globally renowned for its acoustic engineering (the Whispering Gallery).

Additional facts:

3 The central chamber is one of the largest single-chamber spaces in the world, and its dome is frequently cited as the second largest in the world (only behind St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome) and the largest in India.

3 The “Whispering Gallery” runs along the interior base of the dome. Because of the perfect symmetry and the curvature of the dome, a single clap or whisper is reflected multiple times, producing echoes that can be heard up to ten times before fading.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Alauddin Khilji’s market control policies: 1. questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: The Shahna-i-Mandi was the chief superintendent of the central grain market in Delhi. To prevent hoarding and ensure a steady supply at the Sultan’s strictly fixed prices, this official maintained a mandatory register of all the banjaras (itinerant merchants) and wholesale grain dealers. These merchants were compelled to settle near the capital, and their families were often monitored to ensure absolute compliance with the state’s rigorous pricing regulations.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Ziauddin Barani’s Tarikhi-Firoz Shahi is the primary textual source for Alauddin’s market regulations. Barani explicitly details the establishment of the separate markets, the appointed officers, and the price lists. Ibn Battuta visited India decades later during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq; while he noted the lingering legacy of low grain prices in Delhi, he is not the source for the administrative mechanics of Alauddin’s economic policies.

Additional facts:

3 Alauddin Khilji established three distinct and heavily guarded markets in Delhi: one for food grains, a second for costly cloth, sugar, ghee, and oil (known as the Sarai-i-Adl), and a third for horses, slaves, and cattle. Each market operated under its own specific tariff and regulations.

3 To oversee the entire market apparatus and eliminate corruption, Alauddin created an overarching economic department called the Diwan-i-Riyasat. 30

3 The foundational motivation behind these drastic economic measures was military necessity. By forcibly suppressing the prices of all essential commodities to an artificially low rate, Alauddin could afford to pay his massive standing army a very low cash salary, keeping the treasury stable while defending the empire against severe Mongol invasions.

Option D is incorrect: Panhala was a highly strategic defensive stronghold situated in the western Ghats that successfully resisted multiple preliminary Mughal assaults before Aurangzeb finally secured its capitulation later in May 1701 following a comprehensive military encirclement.

Additional facts:

3 Emperor Aurangzeb permanently departed the imperial core of Northern India in 1681, relocating his primary royal encampment to the Deccan for the final twenty-six years of his reign to initially suppress the joint rebellion of his son, Prince Akbar, and the allied Rajput confederacy.

3 Following the capture and execution of Chhatrapati Sambhaji in 1689, the nature of the Maratha conflict transitioned from conventional state warfare into a highly decentralised, agrarian-based insurgency led by autonomous Maratha commanders, most notably Santaji Ghorpade and Dhanaji Jadhav, who utilised rapid light-cavalry tactics to continuously disrupt heavily encumbered Mughal supply lines.

questions.q: Which method allowed Aurangzeb’s forces to capture the fortress of Golconda in 1687?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Option A is correct: After an eight-month siege where the formidable fortress walls successfully withstood continuous heavy artillery bombardment, Aurangzeb ultimately secured victory by heavily bribing a treacherous Afghan noble named Abdullah Pani, who secretly opened the main fortress gate (the Fateh Darwaza) at midnight, allowing the Mughal forces to suddenly enter and overwhelm the garrison.

Option B is incorrect: Although the Mughal engineering corps dug extensive explosive mines beneath the massive granite walls, the highly vigilant Qutb Shahi forces successfully counter-mined these subterranean tunnels, and a catastrophic premature detonation ended up severely damaging the Mughal trenches and killing hundreds of imperial soldiers instead of breaching the fort.

Option C is incorrect: While a devastating famine and a subsequent cholera epidemic ravaged the Mughal military camp stationed directly outside the fort, the well-prepared defenders inside Golconda possessed incredibly ample food stores and granaries, meaning starvation actually threatened to destroy the besieging imperial army far more than it did the trapped garrison.

Option D is incorrect: The traditional siege tactic of escalade (climbing walls using tall wooden ladders) was rendered completely impossible by the vertical height and smooth construction of Golconda’s massive stone battlements, and early, desperate Mughal attempts to physically scale the walls were brutally repulsed by the defenders, ending in disastrous military failures.

Additional facts:

3 The final Mughal campaign to systematically absorb the remaining Deccan sultanates ended with the formal surrender of Sikandar Adil Shah of Bijapur in September 1686, followed exactly a year later by the capture of Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (often referred to as Tana Shah) of Golconda in September 1687.

3 Prior to its annexation, Golconda’s immense economic prosperity and staggering political wealth were heavily sustained by its absolute monopoly over the incredibly lucrative global diamond trade, specifically the Kollur Mine on the banks of the Krishna River, which historically produced world-renowned gems like the Koh-i-Noor and the Hope Diamond.

33

3 During the brutal eight-month siege of Golconda, the heroic defence of the fortress was primarily orchestrated by the fiercely loyal Qutb Shahi military commander Abdur Razzaq Lari, who fought to the end and reportedly sustained over seventy severe sword and lance wounds during the final Mughal breach before finally collapsing.

3 Following the successful capture of the kingdom, Aurangzeb ordered the defeated ruler Abul Hasan Qutb Shah to be permanently imprisoned within the heavily guarded confines of the Daulatabad fort, granting him an imperial state pension of 50,000 rupees annually until his eventual death in captivity.

3 By decisively eliminating the independent, stabilising buffer states of Bijapur and Golconda, Aurangzeb inadvertently brought the sprawling Mughal Empire into direct, unmediated territorial conflict with the highly mobile Maratha light cavalry across the vast, rugged expanses of the Deccan plateau, a monumental strategic miscalculation that overextended imperial supply lines.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Ahom kingdom in Assam: 1. It was founded by Sukapha in the 13th century, and the first capital was at Charaideo. 2. The Ahoms kept detailed historical records called Buranjis. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

Statement 2 is correct: The Ahoms introduced a strong tradition of compiling meticulous historical records. These official state chronicles, known as Buranjis, were initially written in the native TaiAhom language and were later systematically composed in Assamese as the kingdom culturally integrated.

Additional facts:

3 The Ahom economy and military were entirely sustained by the Paik system. Every adult male was registered as a paik and was legally obligated to render rotational labour or military service to the state.

3 The kingdom successfully resisted multiple massive Mughal invasions, most notably defeating the imperial forces at the decisive Battle of Saraighat (1671) under the legendary Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Shahu’s release and its consequences: 1. Prince Azam Shah released Shahu from Mughal captivity in 1707 to intentionally trigger a divisive Maratha civil war. 2. Balaji Vishwanath helped Shahu decisively defeat the rival forces of Tarabai at the Battle of Khed. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
Statement 1 is correct: Following the death of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1707, Prince Azam Shah, acting on the strategic counsel of Zulfiqar Khan, authorised the release of Shahu from the Mughal camp at Doraha. The primary geopolitical objective was to disrupt the unified Maratha resistance led by Tarabai by introducing a legitimate rival claimant to the throne. This calculated move successfully fractured the Maratha state into two warring factions, one centred at Satara under Shahu and the other at Kolhapur under Tarabai, effectively neutralising the Maratha threat to Mughal territories during the ensuing imperial succession struggle.

Statement 2 is correct: Balaji Vishwanath, an influential Chitpavan Brahmin who initially served as a Karkun (revenue official), played a pivotal role in consolidating Shahu’s authority during the civil war. At the Battle of Khed in October 1707, his diplomatic manoeuvring and logistical support were instrumental in Shahu’s victory over Tarabai’s forces. By successfully persuading powerful Maratha commanders like Dhanaji Jadhav to defect from Tarabai’s camp to Shahu’s side, Balaji Vishwanath secured Shahu’s coronation at Satara in 1708 and laid the foundation for his own eventual elevation to the office of Peshwa in 1713.

Additional facts:

3 Despite being a Mughal captive for eighteen years, Shahu was treated with imperial dignity and received a formal Mughal mansab of 7,000, which influenced his later policy of seeking legitimacy through Mughal farmans.

3 The Battle of Khed did not permanently end the conflict; the rivalry persisted until 1731, when the Treaty of Warna formally partitioned the Maratha kingdom into the Northern State (Satara) and the Southern State (Kolhapur).

3 Balaji Vishwanath was officially conferred the title of Sena Karte (Organiser of Armies) by Shahu in recognition of his role in rebuilding the Maratha military administration after the civil war.

34

3 Tarabai’s faction continued to challenge Shahu by declaring him an imperial puppet, forcing Shahu to rely heavily on the Peshwas to establish administrative control over the rebellious Deshmukhs.

3 Shahu’s victory marked a transition from the Chhatrapati-centric administration to a system where the Peshwa emerged as the de facto executive head of the Maratha confederacy.

questions.q: In Mughal agrarian society, what term referred to resident cultivators owning land in their own village?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation:
In the Mughal agrarian system, the term Khudkasht designated resident cultivators who held proprietary rights over the physical land they farmed within their own ancestral village. These primary agriculturalists constituted the rural elite among the peasantry, typically possessing their own essential farming capital, including ploughs, oxen, and seed.

Pahi-kasht referred to non-resident or migrant cultivators who temporarily leased and farmed land in villages other than their own. This class of peasantry was highly mobile, often driven to migrate and seek better revenue terms elsewhere due to localised famines or oppressive tax extraction by regional officials.

Muzarian (plural of muzara) is a generic Persian administrative term broadly translating to a cultivator, tenant, or peasant, functioning as an overarching demographic classification that does not structurally distinguish between a resident landholder and a migrant labourer.

Raiyat (or Ryot) is a broad administrative and legal term referring generally to a revenue-paying subject or peasant. While utilised during the Mughal period to describe the peasantry en masse, it did not specify the socio-economic residency status of the cultivator, and the term was later heavily institutionalised by British colonial administrators.

Additional facts:

3 Khudkasht peasants formed the dominant socio-economic core of the village community, exercising strict customary control over the utilisation of common village lands, pastures, and water resources.

3 Operating outside the traditional village hierarchy, Pahi-kasht peasants functioned on a more contractual basis, negotiating their specific revenue demands and tenancy terms directly with the village headman (muqaddam) or local landowning elites.

3 To maximise agricultural expansion and increase their personal revenue base, local Zamindars actively incentivised Pahi-kasht cultivators to settle and develop newly cleared forests or previously abandoned arable tracts.

3 During periods of severe economic distress, natural calamities, or famine, structural pressures frequently forced established Khudkasht peasants to abandon their ancestral holdings and migrate, thereby transforming them into Pahi-kasht labourers in neighbouring territories.

3 Because continuous cultivation was the fundamental basis of imperial taxation, the Mughal state administration implemented stringent administrative measures—and occasionally utilised localised force, in desperate attempts to prevent Khudkasht peasants from abandoning their highly taxed ancestral lands.

35

Match List-I with List-II

List-II

(Philosophical School) (Propounder) a. Advaita 1. Ramanujacharya b. Vishishtadvaita 2. Madhvacharya c. Dvaita 3. Vallabhacharya d. Shuddhadvaita 4. Adi Shankara Select the correct answer using the codes given below: a b c d
questions.question_type: Match the Following — Two-List Matching — Answer-Code Matrix
questions.explanation:
Adi Shankara propounded Advaita (Absolute Non-Dualism) in the 8th century. He argued that Brahman is the only reality, and the individual soul (Atman) is entirely identical to Brahman. The material world is merely an illusion (Maya).

Ramanuja propounded Vishishtadvaita (Qualified Non-Dualism) in the 11th century. He argued against Adi Shankara’s absolute illusion, stating that while Brahman is the ultimate reality, the individual souls and the material world are real, distinct attributes (or body) of Brahman, completely dependent upon Him but not completely identical.

Madhvacharya propounded Dvaita (Strict Dualism) in the 13th century. He radically opposed Advaita, arguing that Brahman (God), individual souls, and the material world are eternally and fundamentally distinct from one another.

Vallabhacharya propounded Shuddhadvaita (Pure Non-Dualism) in the 15th century. He argued that Brahman is absolutely pure and totally free from Maya. Unlike Adi Shankara, he taught that the physical universe is a real, joyous manifestation of God’s essence, not an illusion.

Additional facts:

3 All of these philosophies are sub-schools of Vedanta (also known as Uttara Mimamsa), which is one of the six orthodox (astika) schools of Hindu philosophy. They all base their arguments on their specific interpretations of the Prasthanatrayi (The Three Sources): The Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras, and the Bhagavad Gita.

3 Other philosophical schools:

Dvaitadvaita (Dualistic Non-Dualism) was propounded by Nimbarkacharya.

Achintya Bheda Abheda (Inconceivable Oneness and Difference) was propounded by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

3 The central, multi-century debate among all these acharyas revolved around a single, highly complex theological problem: What is the exact mathematical and spiritual relationship between God (Brahman), the individual human soul (Jiva), and the physical universe (Jagat)?
